title: Numbers in Both Lists

concept.title: Set intersection
body: The **intersection** of two collections is what they have in common. Put the numbers of the first list into a set. Then go through the second list and keep every number that is in that set. To avoid repeating a number, collect the result in a second set.

Python can write this as `set(a) & set(b)`. The point of the exercise is the idea behind it: membership tests in a hash set are O(1), so the whole job takes O(n + m) instead of comparing every number of `a` with every number of `b`.

statement: Given two lists of integers, print how many different values occur in both lists, and then those values in increasing order.
inputFormat: The second line has the `n` numbers of the first list.
The third line has the `m` numbers of the second list.
outputFormat: The first line: the number `k` of common values.
The second line: the `k` values in increasing order (empty if `k` is 0).

examples.note: The values 4 and 9 occur in both lists.

hints: Put the numbers of one list into a set.
For every number of the other list, check whether it is in the set.
Collect the common values without repeats and sort them at the end.

explanation: Membership in a hash set is O(1), so scanning the second list against a set of the first list finds the common values in linear time.
solution.complexity: Time O(n + m) on average, space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
b = list(map(int, input().split()))

first = set(a)
common = set()
for x in b:
    if x in first:
        common.add(x)
result = sorted(common)
print(len(result))
print(*result)
